name: Piet
title: Programs as paintings
intro: Piet (David Morgan-Mar, 2001, named after the painter Piet Mondrian) uses pictures as source code. The program is a grid of coloured squares called codels. An interpreter walks from one block of colour to the next, and the change in colour between them decides what happens. To play with it, try the npiet interpreter or one of the online Piet editors, which let you paint and step through a program.

lessons.title: Colours and commands
lessons.summary: Hue steps and lightness steps choose the instruction.

sections.p: Piet uses 18 colours: six hues (red, yellow, green, cyan, blue, magenta) in three lightnesses (light, normal, dark), plus white and black. The command is not set by a colour itself but by how far you move between two colours: steps around the hue cycle, and steps darker in lightness (both wrap around).

push pushes the number of codels in the block you just left. A block of 5 red squares followed by a darker red block pushes 5. Arithmetic then works on the stack, like a calculator that uses reverse Polish notation.

The interpreter keeps a direction pointer (right, down, left or up) and a codel chooser (left or right) to decide which edge of a block to leave from. Black squares and the image edge are walls; when every way out is blocked eight times running, the program stops. White is free space that can be crossed without doing anything.

sections.h: How these lessons write a program
sections.p: Each program is drawn in colour and also written out as text, one row per line. Every codel is two letters: the lightness (l light, n normal, d dark) and the hue (r red, y yellow, g green, c cyan, b blue, m magenta). ww is white and kk is black. The run starts at the top-left codel heading right.
sections.code:
lr ly lg lc lb lm
nr ny ng nc nb nm
dr dy dg dc db dm
ww ww ww kk kk kk

practice.q: Light red to normal red. What happens?
practice.why: No hue change and one step darker is push.

practice.q: Red to yellow at the same lightness. What happens?
practice.why: Red to yellow is one hue step with no lightness change: add.

practice.q: What number does push put on the stack?
options: The size of the block just left
practice.answer: The size of the block just left
practice.why: Block size in codels is how Piet gets numbers into a program.
The pointer cannot enter black; it turns and tries another way.

practice.q: Dark red to light red. How many steps darker is that?
practice.why: Lightness wraps around: light, normal, dark, then light again, so dark to light is one step darker.

practice.q: Which change in colour is multiply?
options: One hue step and two darker
practice.answer: One hue step and two darker
practice.why: Look in the hue-step 1 row, two-darker column.

practice.q: How many coloured hues does Piet use (not counting white and black)?
practice.why: Red, yellow, green, cyan, blue and magenta; each comes in three lightnesses.

practice.q: What do the letters ww mean in these lessons?
practice.why: ww is white free space; kk is black.

practice.q: Red to green at the same lightness. What happens?
practice.why: Red to green is two hue steps with no lightness change: divide.

lessons.title: Numbers and arithmetic
lessons.summary: Push block sizes, then add, subtract and multiply.

sections.p: Read this program from the left. The first block has 5 codels; moving from light red to normal red is push, so 5 goes on the stack. The normal red block has 3 codels, and normal red to dark red pushes 3. Dark red to dark yellow is one hue step: add, leaving 8. Dark yellow to light red is five hue steps and one darker: out (number). The white path and the blue bar at the bottom are where the program stops; the last lesson explains how.
sections.code:
lr lr nr dr dy lr kk
lr lr nr kk kk ww kk
lr kk nr kk kk ww kk
kk kk kk kk kk ww kk
kk kk kk kk nb nb nb

sections.p: For subtract, divide and mod, the value pushed first is on the left: push 5, push 3, subtract gives 5 − 3.

lr lr nr kk kk ww kk
lr kk nr kk kk ww kk

lessons.title: Printing characters
lessons.summary: Build a character code, then out (char).

sections.p: out (char) prints the character whose code is on top of the stack. H is 72, which is 8 × 9, so push an 8-codel block and a 9-codel block, multiply, and print.
sections.code:
lr lr lr nr nr nr dr ny lr kk
lr lr lr nr nr nr kk kk ww kk
lr lr kk nr nr nr kk kk ww kk
kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk ww kk
kk kk kk kk kk kk kk nb nb nb

sections.p: i is 105, which is 72 + 33. Duplicate keeps a copy of the 72, the copy is printed, then 3 × 11 = 33 is added to what is left.
sections.code:
lr lr lr nr nr nr dr ny nm lb nb nb nb nb db nm nr lm kk
lr lr lr nr nr nr kk kk kk lb nb nb nb nb kk kk kk ww kk
lr lr kk nr nr nr kk kk kk lb nb nb nb kk kk kk kk ww kk
kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk ww kk
kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk nb nb nb

sections.p: A block of 105 codels works, but most Piet programmers build numbers by multiplying small blocks, just as above. Painting programs that also look good is part of the fun.

practice.q: Which character code does out (char) need to print A?
practice.why: A is 65 in ASCII; 97 is a lowercase a.

practice.q: How would you get 72 on the stack with small blocks?
practice.why: 8 × 9 = 72, using two small blocks instead of one 72-codel block.

options: It prints the top value as a character code
It leaves the value on the stack

sections.p: Roll pops two values: the number of rolls on top, and below it the depth. One roll to depth 3 buries the top value three deep. Push 1, 2, 3, then roll with depth 3 and 1 roll: the stack becomes 3, 1, 2 (top last). Printing three times gives 2, then 1, then 3.

lessons.title: Turning and stopping
lessons.summary: Pointer, white space, and how a program ends.

sections.p: Pointer pops a number and turns the direction pointer clockwise that many times (anticlockwise for a negative number). Here push 1 then pointer turns the run from right to down, and it carries on down the cyan column: push 5, out (number).
sections.code:
lr nr dc kk
kk kk dc kk
kk kk dc kk
kk kk dc kk
kk kk dc kk
kk kk lc kk
kk kk ng kk
kk kk ww kk
kk nb nb nb

sections.p: Moving into white does nothing, and the run slides straight across it to the next colour without running a command. Here the white gap separates two normal red blocks, so nothing happens between them; the second one pushes 4.
sections.code:
lr nr ww ww nr nr dr ny dr kk
lr kk kk kk nr kk kk kk ww kk
lr kk kk kk nr kk kk kk ww kk
kk kk kk kk kk kk kk kk ww kk
kk kk kk kk kk kk kk nb nb nb

sections.p: A program stops when every way out of a block is blocked eight times in a row, with the codel chooser and the direction pointer taking turns to change. The blue bar at the bottom of these programs is entered in the middle from the white path. Its corners are under black codels, and the codel chooser only ever picks the end codels of an edge, so there is no way back up and the run ends.

Switch pops a number and flips the codel chooser that many times. With greater, not, pointer and switch, a program can choose a path depending on a value, and that is how Piet programs loop and decide.

practice.q: What does pointer do with a 1 on the stack?
practice.why: A positive number turns the direction pointer clockwise that many times.

practice.q: What happens when the run crosses white codels?
practice.why: White is free space; only colour-to-colour moves run commands.

practice.q: When does a Piet program stop?
options: After eight blocked attempts in a row
At the last codel of the image
When it reaches a white codel
practice.answer: After eight blocked attempts in a row
practice.why: The interpreter tries every combination of the direction pointer and codel chooser before giving up.
